title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Vronsky and Anna had been traveling together in Europe for three months. They had visited Venice, Rome, and Naples, and had just arrived at a small Italian town where they meant to stay for a while. A handsome head waiter — thick pomaded hair parted from the nape upwards, an evening coat, a broad white cambric shirt front, and a bunch of trinkets hanging above his rounded stomach — was standing with his hands buried in his pockets, his eyes contemptuously half-lidded as he gave some frigid reply to a gentleman who had stopped him. Catching the sound of footsteps coming from the other side of the entry toward the staircase, the head waiter turned, and seeing the Russian count, who had taken their best rooms, he took his hands out of his pockets deferentially, bowed, and told him that a courier had been and that the business about the palazzo was settled. The steward was ready to sign the agreement.
"Ah! I'm glad to hear it," said Vronsky. "Is madame in or out?"
"Madame went out for a walk, but has now returned," the waiter replied.

Vronsky took off his soft, wide-brimmed hat and ran his handkerchief over his hot forehead and over his hair, which had grown halfway over his ears and was brushed back to cover the bald patch. With a casual glance at the gentleman still standing there staring at him, he was about to walk on.
"This gentleman is a Russian, and was asking after you," said the head waiter.

With a mix of annoyance at never being able to escape acquaintances anywhere, and a longing for something to break the monotony of his life, Vronsky looked again at the gentleman, who had backed away and was standing still once more, and at the same instant a light came into both of their eyes.
"Golenishtchev!"
"Vronsky!"

It really was Golenishtchev, a former classmate of Vronsky's in the Corps of Pages. In the corps Golenishtchev had belonged to the liberal party; he had left the corps without going into the army and had never taken a government post. Vronsky and he had gone in completely different directions after leaving the corps, and had only met once since.

At that meeting Vronsky had picked up that Golenishtchev had adopted a sort of lofty, intellectually liberal stance, and was therefore inclined to look down on Vronsky's interests and line of life. Vronsky had accordingly met him with the chilling, haughty manner he knew so well how to put on, the message of which was: "You may like or dislike how I live, that is a matter of perfect indifference to me; you will have to treat me with respect if you want my acquaintance." Golenishtchev had been contemptuously indifferent to the tone Vronsky took. One would have supposed this second meeting would push them further apart still. But here they were, beaming and exclaiming with delight at recognizing one another. Vronsky would never have expected to be so glad to see Golenishtchev, but probably he was not himself aware of how bored he had been. He forgot the disagreeable impression of their last meeting, and with a face of frank delight held out his hand to his old comrade. The same expression of delight replaced the look of unease on Golenishtchev's face.
"How glad I am to see you!" said Vronsky, showing his strong white teeth in a friendly smile.
"I heard the name Vronsky, but I didn't know which one. I'm very, very glad!"
"Let's go in. Come, tell me what you're up to."
"I've been living here for two years. I'm working."
"Ah!" said Vronsky, with sympathy. "Let's go in." And in the habit Russians have of not wanting the servants to overhear what they want to keep private in Russian, he switched into French.
"Do you know Madame Karenina? We're traveling together. I'm just going to see her," he said in French, watching Golenishtchev's face carefully.
"Ah! I didn't know" (though he did know), Golenishtchev answered casually. "Have you been here long?" he added.
"Four days," Vronsky answered, scrutinizing his friend's face again.

"Yes, he's a decent fellow, and will take the thing properly," Vronsky said to himself, catching the meaning of Golenishtchev's expression and his change of subject. "I can introduce him to Anna — he takes the right view."

Over the three months Vronsky had spent abroad with Anna, he had always, on meeting new people, asked himself how the new person would see his relations with Anna, and for the most part, in men, he had been met with the "proper" view of it. But if he had been asked — and if those who took it "properly" had been asked — to spell out exactly how they saw it, both he and they would have been at a loss to answer.

In reality, those who in Vronsky's mind took the "proper" view had no view at all, and were behaving in general the way well-bred people behave toward all the complicated, unsolvable problems life surrounds them with on all sides: behaving with propriety, avoiding allusions and awkward questions. They put on an air of fully grasping the meaning and weight of the situation, of accepting and even approving of it, but of regarding it as superfluous and uncalled-for to put any of this into words.

Vronsky guessed at once that Golenishtchev was of this kind, and was doubly pleased to see him on that account. And in fact Golenishtchev's manner toward Madame Karenina, when he was taken to call on her, was all Vronsky could have wished. He clearly steered clear of any subject that might lead to awkwardness, and without the slightest visible effort.

He had never met Anna before, and was struck by her beauty, and still more by the frankness with which she accepted her position. She blushed when Vronsky brought Golenishtchev in, and he was thoroughly charmed by this childlike blush spreading over her open, handsome face. What he liked particularly was the way she at once — as if on purpose to head off any misunderstanding with an outsider — called Vronsky simply Alexey, and said they were moving into a house they had just taken, what was called here a palazzo. Golenishtchev liked this direct, simple attitude toward her own position. Watching Anna's manner of frank, lively gaiety, and knowing both Alexey Alexandrovitch and Vronsky, Golenishtchev imagined he understood her perfectly. He imagined he understood what she herself was utterly unable to understand: how it was that, having made her husband miserable, having abandoned him and her son and lost her good name, she could still feel full of spirits, gaiety, and happiness.
"It's in the guidebook," said Golenishtchev, referring to the palazzo Vronsky had taken. "There's a first-rate Tintoretto in it. One from his late period."
"I'll tell you what — it's a lovely day, let's go and have another look at it," said Vronsky, turning to Anna.

"I'd love to; I'll just go and put on my hat. Would you say it's hot out?" she said, stopping short in the doorway and giving Vronsky a questioning look. And again a vivid flush spread across her face.
Vronsky saw from her eyes that she did not know on what terms he wished to be with Golenishtchev, and so was afraid of not behaving the way he would want.
He gave her a long, tender look.
"No, not very," he said.
And it seemed to her that she had grasped everything — above all that he was pleased with her; and smiling at him, she walked out the door with her quick step.

The two friends glanced at each other, and a hesitant look came into both their faces, as though Golenishtchev, plainly admiring her, would have liked to say something about her and could not find the right thing to say, while Vronsky both wanted him to say it and dreaded him doing so.

"Well then," Vronsky began, trying to start up some kind of conversation, "so you're settled here? You're still at the same work, then?" he went on, remembering he had heard Golenishtchev was writing something.

"Yes, I'm writing the second part of the _Two Elements_," said Golenishtchev, coloring with pleasure at the question — "that is, to be exact, I'm not writing it yet; I'm preparing, gathering material. It will be on a much wider scale, and will touch on nearly every question. We in Russia refuse to see that we are the heirs of Byzantium," — and he launched into a long, heated exposition of his views.

Vronsky was at first embarrassed at not even knowing about the first part of the _Two Elements_, which the author spoke of as something well known. But as Golenishtchev began laying out his opinions, and Vronsky found he could follow them even without knowing the _Two Elements_, he listened with some interest, because Golenishtchev spoke well. But Vronsky was startled and put off by the nervous irritability with which Golenishtchev talked about the subject that absorbed him. As he went on talking, his eyes glittered angrier and angrier; he was more and more hurried in his replies to imaginary opponents, and his face grew more and more agitated and worried. Remembering Golenishtchev as a thin, lively, good-natured, well-bred boy who was always at the top of the class, Vronsky could not make out why he was so irritated, and he did not like it. What he particularly disliked was that Golenishtchev, a man from a good set, would put himself on the same level with some hack writers, with whom he was irritated and angry. Was it worth it? Vronsky did not like it, but he felt that Golenishtchev was unhappy and was sorry for him. Unhappiness, almost mental disturbance, was visible in his mobile, rather handsome face, while without even noticing Anna's coming in he hurried on hotly setting out his views.

When Anna came in in her hat and cape, her lovely hand swinging her parasol with quick movements, and stood beside him, it was with a feeling of relief that Vronsky tore himself away from Golenishtchev's plaintive eyes, which kept fastening on him, and with a fresh rush of love looked at his charming companion, full of life and happiness. Golenishtchev pulled himself together with an effort, and at first was downcast and gloomy, but Anna, in the mood she was in then to be friendly with everyone, soon revived his spirits with her direct, lively manner. After trying out several subjects, she got him talking about painting, on which he spoke very well, and she listened to him attentively. They walked over to the house they had taken and looked it over.

"I'm so glad of one thing," said Anna to Golenishtchev when they were on the way back. "Alexey will have a wonderful _atelier_. You absolutely must take that room," she said to Vronsky in Russian, using the affectionately familiar form, as if she had seen that Golenishtchev would become close to them in their isolation and there was no point in being reserved in front of him.
"You paint?" said Golenishtchev, turning round quickly to Vronsky.
"Yes, I used to study it long ago, and now I've started doing a bit again," said Vronsky, going red.
"He has great talent," said Anna with a delighted smile. "I'm no judge, of course. But good judges have said the same thing."
